implementation.name: Frege compiler and JVM libraries
implementation.version_scope: Repository documentation and the command-line guide last edited in 2018; no current JDK compatibility claim.

sources.label: Frege language and JVM compilation overview
Frege original and bundled derived-source licenses

fit.text: Frege combines a Haskell-style functional language with Java compilation and access to JVM libraries.

prerequisites.text: Learn lazy functional evaluation and algebraic types; use a JDK with java and javac compatible with the selected compiler jar.

execution.text: The compiler emits Java sources and classes; execution needs the generated class and Frege jar on the JVM classpath.

behavior.text: Types are inferred statically, evaluation is non-strict, and the IO type distinguishes effectful computations from pure values.

tooling.text: The command-line guide covers compilation, generated documentation and property tests through Frege's QuickCheck tools.

maintenance.text: Record the compiler jar and JDK used for a project. The older getting-started guide does not establish compatibility with every newer JDK.

costs.text: Original Frege code uses a BSD-style grant; included Haskell-derived sources carry additional notices and grants.

example.code:
module Hello where
main args = do
    println "PLLDN"
example.run_instructions: Use the chosen compiler jar under the guide's name fregec.jar and create a build directory. Run java -Xss1m -jar fregec.jar -d build Hello.fr, then java -Xss1m -cp "build:fregec.jar" Hello on Unix or java -Xss1m -cp "build;fregec.jar" Hello on Windows.
example.expected_result: The Hello module's main action prints PLLDN.

implementation.name: Futhark compiler with the sequential C backend
implementation.version_scope: Futhark 0.29.0 language reference and C-backend manual checked on 2026-10-13.

sources.label: Futhark functions, types and entry points

fit.text: Futhark expresses array computations for host applications; its GPU backends target computation rather than graphics. This example uses the sequential C backend.

prerequisites.text: Install Futhark and a C compiler available through CC, which defaults to cc. Learn array shapes and functional transformations.

execution.text: futhark c builds an executable or C library. Executables read entry-point arguments from standard input and print returned values in Futhark syntax.

behavior.text: map applies a function to array elements; explicit combinators describe parallel work, while the C backend executes sequential code.

tooling.text: The backend CLI supports library generation, safety checks, diagnostic output and runtime profiling options.

maintenance.text: Keep the chosen backend and entry-point data types explicit; a C-library interface and a standalone executable have different integration workflows.

costs.text: The checked compiler source uses ISC terms. C toolchains, GPU runtimes and drivers remain separate components.

example.run_instructions: Run futhark c increment.fut. Start the generated increment executable and provide [1i32, 2i32, 3i32] as standard input; send end-of-input for your shell.
example.expected_result: Returns an i32 array containing 2, 3 and 4, printed in Futhark syntax.

licenses.notice: ISC applies to the checked Futhark compiler source; it does not establish the terms of every backend dependency.

implementation.name: GAMS modeling system with an LP solver
implementation.version_scope: Documentation as checked on 2026-10-13; no latest-version claim.

sources.label: GAMS CLI, listing and Studio execution
GAMS licensing and permitted evaluation use

fit.text: GAMS represents optimization problems through variables, algebraic equations and an objective, then delegates solution to a selected solver.

prerequisites.text: Formulate constraints and objective first; install GAMS with a valid license and an LP solver permitted by that license.

execution.text: The gams executable compiles and executes a .gms file; a solve statement generates the model and invokes its solver.

behavior.text: =g= expresses a lower-bound constraint, =e= an equality, and variable .l values report solution levels after solving.

tooling.text: GAMS Studio, command-line logs and listing files expose equations, model statistics and solver results.

maintenance.text: Inspect both model and solver status before using reported values. Validate generated equations against the intended mathematical model.

costs.text: Demo licenses permit limited initial exploration and exclude commercial or production use; applicable professional and solver entitlements must be checked.

example.run_instructions: With a valid GAMS license and an available LP solver, run gams minimum.gms. Inspect the listing's solve summary and displayed variable levels.
example.expected_result: For an optimal solve, x.l and z.l are 2. Compilation or solver completion alone does not establish optimality.

licenses.scope: GAMS system entitlement described by its licensing page; selected solvers and edition-specific agreements must be checked separately.

implementation.name: GAP core computational algebra system
implementation.version_scope: Documentation as checked on 2026-10-13; no latest-version claim.

sources.label: GAP computational algebra and source overview
GAP first-session and source loading tutorial

fit.text: GAP supports computational discrete algebra, particularly group theory, with algebraic objects and algorithms rather than general application frameworks.

prerequisites.text: Install GAP and understand the algebraic objects being modeled; the tutorial starts with interactive commands and source-file loading.

execution.text: The gap command starts an interpreter; Read loads a source file into the session and quit exits it.

behavior.text: Permutations use cycle notation. Group constructs a generated group and Size counts its elements; double semicolons suppress automatic display.

tooling.text: The interactive environment includes help, algebraic computations and separately distributed packages.

maintenance.text: Document the group representation and packages used. Stored attributes and session variables can affect subsequent interactive computations.

costs.text: GAP core's source grant is GPL-2.0-or-later; separately distributed packages require their own license checks.

example.run_instructions: Start gap in the directory containing group.g, enter Read("group.g"); and finish the session with quit;.
example.expected_result: Prints 6, the order of the permutation group generated by a transposition and a three-cycle.

licenses.scope: The named implementation only; dependencies and host runtimes have separate terms.
licenses.notice: GAP's README grants GPL version 2 or later for GAP core. Package-specific and external-library terms are not inferred from that grant.

implementation.name: Godot Engine's GDScript implementation
implementation.version_scope: Godot 4.x stable GDScript and standalone SceneTree script documentation as checked; this is not a Godot 3 workflow.

sources.label: Godot command-line tutorial: standalone scripts and headless execution
Godot: engine licensing and third-party attribution

fit.text: Script game and interactive application behavior inside Godot's node and scene model. GDScript is integrated with Godot rather than a Python interpreter.

prerequisites.text: Install a matching Godot 4.x engine/editor and learn nodes, resources, classes and functions. A standalone command-line script must extend SceneTree or MainLoop.

execution.text: Godot loads .gd scripts. A SceneTree script can run through --script; --headless supplies a command-line workflow without a graphical window.

behavior.text: GDScript uses indentation-based syntax and supports optional type annotations. Its engine objects and built-in types follow Godot's APIs.

tooling.text: Use Godot's editor and command-line options. --check-only with --script parses for errors; executing a script is a separate operation.

maintenance.text: Keep scripts aligned with the Godot version and project resources. Exporting a game also requires the chosen export preset and templates.

costs.text: Plan for engine, export and asset requirements. Godot's own MIT notice and third-party engine or asset notices need separate attention.

example.code:
extends SceneTree

func _init() -> void:
    print("PLLDN")
    quit()
example.run_instructions: Save hello.gd and, using a Godot 4.x executable available as godot, run godot --headless --script hello.gd. The script extends SceneTree and quits after printing.
example.expected_result: The output includes a line containing PLLDN, then the engine exits; startup information may also be printed.

licenses.scope: Godot's own code; the engine bundles third-party components with additional notices.
licenses.notice: Provide the required engine license notice and review the engine distribution's third-party notices and your project's assets separately.

fit.text: GLSL defines shader-stage computations for graphics and compute pipelines. This profile uses glslang to validate a fragment shader and generate SPIR-V.

prerequisites.text: Install a glslang build with SPIR-V support; understand fragment outputs and the host pipeline that consumes them.

execution.text: glslang selects stage rules from the file extension; -V generates Vulkan-targeted SPIR-V and -o names its output file.

behavior.text: Variables have declared types; vector outputs and interface locations connect shader computations to the surrounding pipeline.

tooling.text: The standalone compiler reports shader errors; its APIs also expose syntax trees and source-level reflection.

maintenance.text: Choose the shader version, stage and target semantics explicitly. Compilation validates source without demonstrating rendering in a host application.

costs.text: glslang's license file identifies multiple grants and external components; redistribution must preserve applicable notices. GPU drivers and host libraries have separate terms.

example.run_instructions: Run glslang -V color.frag -o color.spv with a SPIR-V-enabled build. Rendering additionally requires a host pipeline with a compatible fragment-output attachment; this file alone does not open a window.
example.expected_result: Successful compilation writes color.spv. In a compatible host pipeline, the fragment shader outputs the constant RGBA vector (0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.0).

implementation.name: Cucumber Gherkin parser with Cucumber.js runner
implementation.version_scope: Current Gherkin reference and Cucumber.js main documentation as checked; choose installed-package documentation when runner versions differ.

sources.label: Cucumber: Gherkin grammar and step definitions
Cucumber.js: project structure and running features

fit.text: Describe acceptance scenarios in structured natural language for executable specifications. Gherkin records scenarios; application actions live in separate step-definition code.

prerequisites.text: Learn Feature, Scenario and Given/When/Then syntax. Running scenarios requires a chosen Cucumber implementation and step definitions matching the step text.

execution.text: A runner parses .feature files and connects steps to implementation code. Without matching definitions, a feature does not become a passing application test.

behavior.text: Keywords structure scenarios, backgrounds and outlines. Step text is matched to definitions; prose descriptions are documentation rather than executed actions.

tooling.text: Cucumber.js uses a Node.js environment and the cucumber-js CLI; its project separates feature files from JavaScript support code.

maintenance.text: Version feature files with the application and keep step definitions aligned with business behavior. Runner main documentation can include unreleased changes.

costs.text: Budget for runner setup, test infrastructure and step-definition maintenance. Parser and runner grants do not cover the application, Node.js or every dependency.

example.code:
Feature: Greeting
  Scenario: A greeting is available
    When the greeter supplies a message
    Then the message should be "PLLDN"
example.run_instructions: In a Cucumber.js project with a supported Node.js runtime, save this as features/hello.feature and run npx cucumber-js. Implement matching When and Then definitions in features/support before expecting a passing test. The feature alone deliberately contains no application implementation.
example.expected_result: Without matching support code the runner reports undefined steps. With definitions that provide and check the stated message, the scenario can verify that behavior.

licenses.scope: The parser source in cucumber/gherkin; this is not a license assigned to your feature files.
licenses.notice: Retain the MIT notice for redistributed parser material and inspect its dependencies.

licenses.scope: The JavaScript test runner source; Node.js and application dependencies are separate.
licenses.notice: Retain the MIT notice for covered runner material and review the complete installed test environment.

implementation.name: gnuplot plotting interpreter with the dumb terminal
implementation.version_scope: Documentation as checked on 2026-10-13; no latest-version claim.

sources.label: gnuplot manual source and scripting commands

fit.text: gnuplot plots mathematical functions and data through command scripts; the selected dumb terminal produces a text plot.

prerequisites.text: Install gnuplot and learn function expressions, plotting ranges and output-terminal selection; this example requires no input data file.

execution.text: gnuplot can read a command file or evaluate commands supplied on its CLI; a terminal determines the output representation.

behavior.text: sin uses radians by default. plot samples the selected range; terminal size controls the text block rather than numerical precision.

tooling.text: Interactive commands, script files and selectable terminals support repeatable plotting workflows.

maintenance.text: Record ranges, data transforms and terminal choices with the script; output layout depends on the selected terminal.

costs.text: The gnuplot grant permits use and distribution subject to notices, and imposes specific conditions on distributing modified versions.

example.code:
set terminal dumb size 60,15
set title "Sine wave"
plot [0:6.28] sin(x) title "sin(x)"
example.run_instructions: Run gnuplot wave.gp from the directory containing the script; the dumb terminal writes an ASCII plot to the terminal.
example.expected_result: Displays a text plot of approximately one sine-wave period over the interval 0 to 6.28.
